title: Character study
text: CHARACTER STUDY STEVENS Stevens is the head butler of Darlington Hall and the protagonist-narrator of the novel. In the present moment of the novel, he is a man in the latter half of his life. His employer Mr Farraday remarks to him at the beginning of the novel that he looks like he could “make good use of a break,” indicating to us that he has a somewhat fatigued and elderly appearance (p. 3). Stevens is an exceptionally hard-working individual. He is calculating and deliberate in his actions, and professional to the point where we begin to lose sight of his emotional dimension, as he is so strictly focused only on professional matters. Stevens is polite, courteous, and loyal. On occasion he is unaware of social cues, and the ability to be humorous in the company of others does not come naturally to him. He is a modest figure who enjoys simple pleasures such as the charms a small English village might offer, like a picturesque stone footbridge or a peaceful stream. Ultimately, two of Stevens’ defining characteristics are his traditionalism and his optimism: he is a believer in continual self-improvement and deems it within one’s capability to strive for greatness. This trait is illustrated by the light-hearted ending of the novel in which Stevens looks forward to returning to Darlington Hall to sharpen his bantering skills. MISS KENTON Miss Kenton is the head housekeeper at Darlington Hall and Stevens’ closest acquaintance. As the novel progresses, we see her relationship with Stevens evolve, although it remains professional. Like Stevens, Miss Kenton takes her work very seriously and executes her duties with efficiency and skill, but in contrast to him she is a more lively and colourful character. Interestingly, one of the first memories of Miss Kenton that Stevens recalls tells of how she entered his room with flowers to brighten up his dimly-lit and bare parlour. This symbolic act serves to illustrate how Miss Kenton brings vibrancy, beauty and (literally) colour into Stevens’ life. Miss Kenton is inquisitive and occasionally stubborn and defiant in face of authority, as shown by her challenging Stevens when he asks her to ‘speak up’ to his father, who is in fact in a subordinate position to her. Miss Kenton leaves Darlington Hall to pursue what will end up as an unhappy marriage, and she tenderly and nostalgically reflects on what her life would have been like had she stayed at Darlington Hall in close proximity to Stevens. LORD DARLINGTON Lord Darlington is the owner of Darlington Hall and the former employer of Stevens and the rest of the staff in the interwar period. He is a tall, slender man in his mid-fifties. Lord Darlington is a symbol of tradition, and stands for the values of trust, honour and morality. We learn through Stevens’ writings that Lord Darlington fought for the alleviation of the punishment that was forced upon Germany following its defeat in World War I. Lord Darlington’s sympathy towards the Germans continued into the 1930s as he contributed to the appeasement of the Nazis, a decision that was based on a desire for peace but ended up being disastrously short-sighted. Lord Darlington is a character of high moral stature, but in the context of a hostile and dangerous international climate which requires savvy diplomacy, he is perhaps too enmeshed in the old traditional value system based on honour and trust. MR FARRADAY Mr Farraday is a wealthy American gentleman who at the outset of the novel has become the new proprietor of Darlington Hall and thus Stevens’ new employer. Mr Farraday offers a contrast to Stevens and Lord Darlington and the solidity of English ritual that they represent. For example, his more casual and informal manner of interacting with the staff, shown by his encouragement of Stevens to take off time for himself and his bantering with him over inappropriate topics, troubles Stevens. Mr Farraday marks the passage of the time and the emergence of a newer generation freed from the tight reins of traditional professionalism.
